pending_articles.title: Coordination without command: active inference and the route to embodied intelligence
pending_articles.content: Embodied intelligence depends on bodies whose contact with the environment, distribution of load and capacity for action are only partly known and are changed by movement. We argue that this creates a practical reason to organize inference through distributed, hierarchical and plural processes, using active inference to relate local belief updating, contextual constraints and action selection within a common framework. The proposal brings together established ideas from factorized inference, distributed control and embodied robotics, distinguishing their mathematical description from the location of computation and authority over action. The octopus provides biological motivation through its combination of peripheral sensorimotor processing and central influences on behavior, while an articulated hexapod illustrates selected architectural choices through six leg-local predictive controllers coupled by neighbor messages and a shared mechanical body. The simulation includes intact locomotion and movement following programmed limb withdrawal and graph reconfiguration, although these observations do not isolate the contribution of inference or establish remapping. Together, the biological example and computational illustration clarify how local inferential processes may remain coordinated across bodily interfaces and timescales without a controller prescribing the complete joint trajectory.

pending_articles.title: What shared responses reveal about audience behavior: neural prediction and the emerging potential of peripheral synchrony
pending_articles.content: Predicting audience responses to dynamic media remains a significant challenge in neuromarketing and neuroforecasting. Intersubject correlation (ISC) has been proposed to address this need by quantifying the temporal similarity of neural, physiological, and behavioral responses among individuals exposed to the same stimulus. This narrative mini-review examines how ISC relates to preferences, judgments, and behavior and proposes a conceptual framework for interpreting its predictive value. Across modalities, ISC consistently reflects shared stimulus processing and is associated with attention, alongside additional links to engagement, memory, and higher-order narrative processing. Neural ISC has shown associations with individual, group, and population-level outcomes, although findings vary by neural modality, analytic approach, and behavioral endpoint. Peripheral ISC derived from gaze, heart rate, electrodermal activity, and facial expressions provides complementary information about interindividual alignment, but direct evidence for predicting consumer outcomes remains limited. At the same time, neural and peripheral measures capture various aspects of shared response dynamics, and combining them in a multimodal ISC approach may help distinguish synchronization in different functional domains, including perceptual, attentional, autonomic, affective, and valuation-related processes, and clarify their relationship to the target outcome. The proposed framework therefore conceptualizes ISC as a probabilistic predictor whose predictive value depends on which functional processes underlie the observed synchrony and their relevance to the specific outcome of interest.

pending_articles.title: Case Report: Clinical applications of extended-duration remote ambulatory EEG monitoring: lessons from real-world cases
pending_articles.content: BackgroundTraditional ambulatory electroencephalography (EEG) and inpatient epilepsy monitoring unit (EMU) admissions face significant operational limitations including: short recording windows (typically 24–72 h), high costs, technician shortages, and physical restrictions on daily activities.MethodsThis article presents clinical utility frameworks and three illustrative real-world case studies utilizing the REMI Remote EEG Monitoring System—a wireless, wearable 4-sensor electrode-setup (10-channel EEG montage system) montage system integrated with cloud data transmission and post-acquisition artificial intelligence (AI) electrographic seizure detection algorithms.ResultsIn Case 1, a 39-year-old female with suspected recurrent epilepsy experienced three focal seizures after the standard 72-h monitoring window, allowing initiation of targeted antiseizure therapy. In Case 2, extended monitoring in a 57-year-old male with long-standing epilepsy experiencing new exercise-induced symptoms ruled out electrographic seizures, avoiding unnecessary medication escalation. In Case 3, a 52-year-old male with worsening episodic déjà vu exhibited focal interictal rhythmic activity, providing objective data to guide shared decision-making and successful initiation of antiseizure treatment.ConclusionExtended-duration remote EEG monitoring bridges key diagnostic gaps by offering flexible, real-world data collection over extended timeframes (up to 30 days). This approach optimizes clinical triage, clarifies event etiology, and improves ambulatory epilepsy care without overburdening tertiary health care infrastructure.

recently_processed.title: When neuroscience meets machine learning: a taxonomic scoping review of machine and statistical learning approaches in sub-Saharan Africa
recently_processed.content: In high-resource economies, computational neuroscience research frequently employs machine learning (ML) and statistical learning (SL) techniques. While these methods provide effective ways to analyse multimodal, high-dimensional, and complex data they are underexplored in low resource settings. This taxonomic scoping review uses a systematic methodological approach to synthesise the application of ML and SL techniques in neuroscience research in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to discussing findings, strengths, limitations, and future prospects, the work classifies current research by neuroscience domains, applications, learning tasks, datasets, tools, and techniques. In order for African researchers to contribute to and benefit from the global computational neuroscience landscape, our review contends that low- and middle-income countries must create and augment context-specific and representative datasets and incorporate appropriate features for model training. Future studies should focus on pragmatic rather than complex modelling, external validation, reproducibility, interpretability, and utilise real-world data to determine clinical utility.

recently_processed.title: Validation of the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised in patients with disorders of consciousness
recently_processed.content: ObjectiveOur objective was to validate the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R).DesignWe conducted a multicenter study across neurology, intensive care, neuro-rehabilitation, and nursing departments in Hungary. Thirty-one patients (17 males; mean age 49.1 ± 16.1 years) with disorders of consciousness (DOC) following severe acquired brain injury were assessed. Two independent raters reassessed the same patients within a one-week window to evaluate inter-rater and intra-rater reliability. We assessed reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa and evaluated concurrent validity using Spearman’s rank correlation.ResultsConcurrent validity with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was strong across all raters and time points (rho = 0.882–0.934, p < 0.001). Inter-rater reliability for the total score was excellent at initial assessment (wk = 0.977) and remained high at follow-up (wk = 0.977). Diagnostic classification agreement between raters was nearly perfect (wk = 0.936–1.000).ConclusionThe Hungarian CRS-R is a valid and reliable instrument that preserves the robustness of the original version. Its implementation fills a critical gap in national healthcare by providing an evidence-based tool to reduce DOC misdiagnosis rates.
